0.content: While investigating rainforest ruins at Tighnari's invitation, Faruzan overheard someone praying earnestly to the Dendro Archon to learn words faster. She decided at once that this was a student of "suitable age, fitting direction, and excellent quality" and stepped out from behind a tree. Collei squeaked in fright, and Tighnari had to clear up the misunderstanding. Faruzan has wanted to teach her ever since. She brings Collei food at Gandharva Ville, tells her not to let Tighnari know, scolds Tighnari over Collei's eye bags, and calls her respectful, diligent and perfect. She does not quite realise what else draws her: Collei suffered terribly and still found the strength to face life.

1.content: Tighnari treats Faruzan as a true senior researcher "in every sense of the word". He invited her to survey rainforest ruins, and in the 3.5 hangout he asked her to repair Karkata because Kshahrewar and Spantamad scholars were too prejudiced to trust. He tells the Traveler the story of her entrapment so that Faruzan doesn't have to, and warns that she doesn't want pity. She calls him "that brat", enjoys travelling with "the living copy of the Rainforest Survival Guide", and says he has eaten more kinds of fungi than she has.

2.comment: Faruzan: The Century in the Ruin
2.content: About a hundred years ago Faruzan miscalculated while solving a puzzle in a King Deshret ruin filled with mechanisms and coded inscriptions, and was trapped. A mysterious power kept her body in stasis: no hunger, no physical fatigue, but no escape from mental wear. She used up her paper without translating a single line, then carved deductions into the floor with broken stone so the next trapped person might have a chance. When the floor was full she calculated in her head. Her memory blurred and she began muttering. At some point she solved it, though she no longer remembers how. Wind met her at the exit, and she followed it, with her new Vision, until she collapsed from hunger. A caravan found her by her glittering Vision.

3.comment: Faruzan: Tamimi and the Last Letters
3.content: In her Hangout Event (3.5), Faruzan, the Traveler and an archaeologist named Raed found a huge machine wreck in the Hypostyle Desert. Faruzan saw that it was only about a dozen years old and decoded Raed's "excavation records", in which "tents" was code for relics he was selling. When the wreck reactivated and chased the diggers, she realised it was Tamimi, the small mechanical life form that once took her notes and carried her letters home. Her teacher and friends had rebuilt it to learn and repair itself, and it had searched the ruins for decades, growing into the legendary "Ruin Wanderer", to deliver their letters. Her mother's ends: "Welcome home, Faruzan." Tamimi's overworked heart gave out after it found her.

4.content: Faruzan's field is "the analysis of the structure of and solutions to various ruin devices via the study of stone carvings and other ancient texts", so it is linguistics applied to mechanisms. A century ago it was vital; now Kshahrewar's mechanics have matured and few ruins remain unexplored. Haravatat reviewers reject her topics and cut her funding, and students fall asleep in her lectures. Kshahrewar, whose students graduated on her manuscripts, keeps offering better terms. One recruiter who said "the era of interpreting ancient texts is over" was lectured for the length of two classes and drank himself sorry at Lambad's Tavern. A Haravatat friend who set out to debate "this old fogey" ended up the same way the next night.

5.comment: Faruzan: Cyno and the Vairambhaka Gear
5.content: The Vairambhaka Gear, a "multi-purpose ruin exploration auxiliary support terminal", was one of the few projects the Akademiya funded after her return. Matra stormed her workshop, suspecting her silence about her disappearance and her refusal to join Kshahrewar hid a dangerous machine. General Mahamatra Cyno arrived, cleared her with records, apologised and left a matra to help tidy up. Pleased, she invited him to name the machine. He proposed "Great Vayuvyastra", which baffled her; a matra noted Kshahrewar already had a machine by that name. She studied how such names are formed and chose "Vairambhaka" herself.
